content_text: Don Miguel Ruiz - "The Voice of Knowledge" This was a surprisingly impactful book that changed my worldview I'd start with "Four Agreements" which is better known and, to me, is a must-read (both books are short, 100-150 pages) Voice of Knowledge was the book that introduced me to the following framework. 1/5 INTRO: DIRECT EXCERPT I will give an off-the-cuff summary, with an intro that is a direct quote: “You are the author of an ongoing story you tell yourself. In your story, everything is about you, and it has to be that way because you are the center of your perception. The story is told from your point of view. You create an image for the secondary characters in your story, and you assign them a role to play. The only thing you know about the secondary characters is the story you create about them. The truth is that you don’t know anyone, and nobody knows you either… it’s not important to be right or to make others wrong. Instead, you see everybody as an artist, a storyteller. You know that whatever they believe is just their point of view. It has nothing to do with you.” 1/5 >Everything we think and say is a story based on our point of view >What we know about ourselves, is simply an assemblage of stories that we have put together about who we are >Note that there is minimal, if any, truth to any of these stories. >At any point you can rip apart these stories, your self-image, and create new ones 2/5 >At the same time, everyone you see around you, is a story to you >At the same time, you are a story to them >Note that all of these stories -- yours of them, theirs of you -- may have no basis in factual reality. >Once you internalize this framework, and you listen to people as they speak, you will see the truth of it >People have built up these elaborate defense mechanisms, stories, about what they can and can't do, self-limiting beliefs, load-bearing delusions, and "stories" of who they are that are so deeply wound >Yet you can't help but laugh because you see it as, like, there is absolutely nothing permanent to ANY of these stories you have of yourself. 3/5 >There are people who have a story of you -- say, where you are the villian in their story -- and there's nothing you can do to change their story. >Similarly, to others you may be a hero, who can do no wrong -- they are wrong as well, but again, you are powerless to change their story (think of a mother's love for their child). >Once you recognize this truth of the world for what it is, you find yourself detatching from several elements of reality >First, you find yourself questioning: what are these stories I believe about myself? Where did they come from? You will find they are surprisingly pliable and usually built on a house of cards. >Your self-image is something you can knock down and rebuild. Just because you have been a loser your whole life, doesn't mean that tomorrow, you can destroy that "I'm a loser" self-image and create a new one. 4/5 >Similarly, you worry less about what people think of you and why. By now, you may have realized there are some people who, no matter what you do, they will NEVER like you. On the same token, to some people you can do no wrong. But their stories of you, these are out of your control. So let them live their story out, you can't change it for them. >Relationships become clearer once you stop trying to force a preconceived story of who you want them to be on them. Most relationships in your past have failed because you had a story of who you wanted them to be, and they failed to live up to it. That's your fault -- not theirs. >Most of your misery is based on some preconceived story of who you are supposed to be, and failing to live up to this fabricated and unrealistic notion. By asking "where does this voice come from" and dismantling it for the phantasm as it is, you will realize that you have been worshipping false idols, pressed upon you by others, by the world, by society, by unfair expectations of others...and only then, when you realize all these stories (others' of you, and yours of yourself), will you begin to start living a life authentic to yourself. 5/5 That was my off-the-cuff read of the book. The TL;DR is that everyone and everything is stories. You are a story of yourself. Others are a story you fabricrated of them. In exchange, you may notice how all people see you in different lights -- this is proof of concept, that you are not ONE person, but some mix of stories that others conjure of you, based on their own beliefs and biases and upbringings. In understanding this, you take the words of others less seriously, and you give yourself more room to reinvent yourself at will. END I thought this was a very accurate worldview, one which I doubt Ruiz invented, but he was the first to bring it to my attention. This will drastically reduce the amount of stress in your life as you learn to recognize that someone is simply projecting a strange and toxic story -- deflecting and projecting -- based on their own past, onto you. Don't take it personal. Live your own truth. GB
